warmup.q: A flow reads a settlement line every 100 ms and emits it. The collector needs 300 ms to post each line to the ledger. There is no buffer. When does the second emit happen?
options: At t=200 ms: the producer keeps reading while the collector works
At t=400 ms: right after the first posting finishes
At t=500 ms: the first posting finishes at 400, then the producer needs 100 ms more
At t=300 ms: the two sides overlap halfway
warmup.why: emit(1) is called at 100 ms and does not return until the collector has posted the line at 400 ms. Only then does the producer read the next line, which takes another 100 ms. The answer t=200 assumes emit drops the value into a queue, which a plain flow never does.

sections.h: A reader and a ledger writer: predict the print order
sections.html:
Here is a settlement-file reader feeding a ledger writer through a flow. Before you read on, write down the order of the lines it prints.

Java
// Java equivalent: Java has no Flow, so this is a hand-written push "flow".
// The reader calls the ledger writer's Consumer once per line.
static void readSettlementFile(List<String> lines, Consumer<String> ledgerWriter) {
    for (String line : lines) {
        String id = line.substring(0, line.indexOf(','));
        System.out.println("read    " + id);
        ledgerWriter.accept(id);
        System.out.println("accept(" + id + ") returned");
    }
}

readSettlementFile(lines, id -> System.out.println("posted  " + id));
Kotlin
val records = flow {
    for (line in lines) {                    // "pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,990,EUR", "pay-3,12000,GBP"
        val id = line.substringBefore(",")
        println("read    $id")
        emit(id)
        println("emit($id) returned")
    }
}
println("flow built")
records.collect { id -> println("posted  $id") }
println("collect returned")

Two guesses are tempting. One says all three read lines come first and then the three posted lines, as if emit dropped the value into a queue for later. The other gets the pairs right but prints emit(pay-1) returned before posted pay-1, as if emit handed the value over and moved on. Here is the real output:

flow built
read    pay-1
posted  pay-1
emit(pay-1) returned
read    pay-2
posted  pay-2
emit(pay-2) returned
read    pay-3
posted  pay-3
emit(pay-3) returned
collect returned

flow built comes first, so building the flow ran none of its body. And posted pay-1 comes before emit(pay-1) returned: the ledger writer's code ran while emit was still running. There is no queue here and no second thread.

Lesson 7 of the coroutines track gave you three rules about flows. They are cold, they run one value at a time, and a slow collector slows the producer. All three come from a single fact: emit is a plain function call into the collector. About ten lines of code are enough to prove it. The Java version prints the same order for the same reason. accept is a method call, and the line after a call runs when the call returns.

The Java twin prints the same pattern with accept(...) returned: a Consumer call behaves the same way.

sections.h: Two interfaces and a three-line builder
sections.html:
A flow needs a receiving end and a sending end. Each is a single suspend function.

Java
// Java equivalent: the same two interfaces, with plain blocking methods
interface ToyCollector<T> {
    void emit(T value);
}

interface ToyFlow<T> {
    void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector);    // one abstract method, so a lambda is a ToyFlow
}
Kotlin
fun interface ToyCollector<in T> {
    suspend fun emit(value: T)
}

interface ToyFlow<out T> {
    suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>)
}

fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> =
    object : ToyFlow<T> {
        override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block()
    }

The builder is the whole trick. toyFlow { ... } stores your block in an object and returns it. Nothing runs. When someone calls collect(collector), the object runs your block with that collector as the receiver. So every emit(x) inside the block is really collector.emit(x): a direct call into the collector's code.

Use it like the real thing:

Java
ToyFlow<Integer> payments = collector -> {
    for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) {
        System.out.println("  [producer] before emit(" + id + ")");
        collector.emit(id);
        System.out.println("  [producer] after emit(" + id + ")");
    }
};
System.out.println("built the flow, nothing ran yet");
payments.collect(v -> System.out.println("  [collector] got " + v));
payments.collect(v -> System.out.println("  [collector] got " + v));   // the body runs again
Kotlin
val payments = toyFlow {
    for (id in 1..3) {
        println("  [producer] before emit($id)")
        emit(id)
        println("  [producer] after emit($id)")
    }
}
println("built the flow, nothing ran yet")
payments.collect { v -> println("  [collector] got $v") }
payments.collect { v -> println("  [collector] got $v") }   // the body runs again

Building prints nothing. The first collect runs the body, and each before emit(n) is followed by got n and only then by after emit(n). That's the same pattern the settlement reader printed. The second collect runs the whole body again from the top. That is all cold means: a flow is a function you haven't called yet, and collect calls it.

The Java twin has the same shape and prints the same lines. What differs is the cost of waiting. Java's emit is an ordinary call, so while the collector works, the producer's thread sits inside emit and can do nothing else. Kotlin's emit is a suspend call. If the collector calls delay or waits on a socket, the coroutine suspends and the thread goes off to run other coroutines. The order of events is the same in both.

steps: Open ToyFlow.kt in the demo folder. It holds the two interfaces, the builder, a toy map and a main. Predict how many [producer] start lines it prints.
Run it. Check that built the flow, nothing ran yet comes before any producer line.
Add a third collection at the end of main: payments.map { it + 1 }.map { it * 2 }.collect { println(it) }. Predict the values and the number of [producer] start lines, then run it.

code.title: ToyFlow.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking // A flow from scratch: two interfaces and a three-line builder. No kotlinx.coroutines flow types. // StackDemo.kt and Backpressure.kt in this folder use these too. fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } /** map is a collector wrapped in a collector. */ fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val payments = toyFlow { println(" [producer] start") for (id in 1..3) { println(" [producer] before emit($id)") emit(id) println(" [producer] after emit($id)") } println(" [producer] done") } println("built the flow, nothing ran yet") println("--- first collect, through map") payments.map { it * 100 }.collect { v -> println(" [collector] got $v") } println("--- second collect: the body runs again") payments.collect { v -> println(" [collector] got $v") } }

alt.title: ToyFlowJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ToyFlow.kt: the same two interfaces, pushing values with a plain method call. // One difference: this emit blocks the thread while the collector works. In Kotlin emit is a // suspend call, so a collector that waits (delay, I/O) gives the thread back meanwhile. package workbench.flows.l01; import java.util.function.Function; public class ToyFlowJava { interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } // one abstract method, so Java takes a lambda for it interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); // map is a collector wrapped in a collector default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ToyFlow<Integer> payments = collector -> { System.out.println(" [producer] start"); for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) { System.out.println(" [producer] before emit(" + id + ")"); collector.emit(id); System.out.println(" [producer] after emit(" + id + ")"); } System.out.println(" [producer] done"); }; System.out.println("built the flow, nothing ran yet"); System.out.println("--- first collect, through map"); payments.map(id -> id * 100).collect(v -> System.out.println(" [collector] got " + v)); System.out.println("--- second collect: the body runs again"); payments.collect(v -> System.out.println(" [collector] got " + v)); } }

Your third collection starts the body a third time and prints 4, 6 and 8: each value goes through both maps inside one emit call before the producer reads the next. The Java twin prints the same lines as the original Kotlin program.

sections.h: The collector runs inside emit: read the stack
sections.html:
You can see the call shape for yourself. Print the stack from inside the collector:

Java
static void printStack(String label) {
    System.out.println(label + ", thread=" + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    StackTraceElement[] frames = Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace();
    for (int i = 2; i < frames.length; i++)
        System.out.println("    at " + frames[i].getClassName() + "." + frames[i].getMethodName());
}

ToyFlow<String> payments = collector -> collector.emit("pay-1");
payments.collect(value -> printStack("collector got " + value));
Kotlin
fun printStack(label: String) {
    println("$label, thread=${Thread.currentThread().name}")
    Thread.currentThread().stackTrace.drop(2)
        .takeWhile { !it.className.startsWith("kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask") }
        .forEach { println("    at ${it.className}.${it.methodName}") }
}

toyFlow { emit("pay-1") }.collect { printStack("collector got $it") }

For the toy flow it prints this, newest call on top (I trimmed the package names):

collector got pay-1, thread=main
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$2.emit             <- your collector lambda
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$2.emit
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invokeSuspend    <- the toyFlow { } block, calling emit
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invoke
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$1.invoke
    at ToyFlowKt$toyFlow$1.collect           <- ToyFlow.collect, running the block
    at StackDemoKt$main$1.invokeSuspend      <- main, calling collect

Read it from the bottom. main called collect. collect ran the block. The block called emit, and emit is your lambda. It is all one thread. The real flow { }.map { } gives a taller stack with the same shape (here I also dropped repeated frames and two helper frames):

collector got PAY-1, thread=main
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$5.emit                                   <- your lambda
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$invokeSuspend$$inlined$map$1$2.emit      <- map's collector
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.internal.SafeCollector.emit         <- a checker
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$3.invokeSuspend                          <- your flow { } block
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.SafeFlow.collectSafely
    at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.AbstractFlow.collect
    at StackDemoKt$main$1$invokeSuspend$$inlined$map$1.collect     <- map's collect
    at StackDemoKt$main$1.invokeSuspend                            <- main

map is an inline function, so its collector is compiled into your own file. SafeCollector is a checker that flow { } puts in front of your collector. Lesson 2 of this track opens it up.

Here is the picture to keep. A plain flow is a small restaurant with one cook and no counter. The cook plates a dish (emit), walks it to the table, and stands there while the diner eats (your collector). Only when the diner is done does the cook walk back and plate the next one. A map is a waiter between them, and the waiter stands at the table too. In the stack, each of them is a box inside the one before.

sections.h: Cold, sequential and slowed by its collector, all from one call
sections.html:
The rules you learned about flows all follow from that stack.

A flow is cold because the block is the body of collect. No collect, no run. Two collect calls, two runs.

A flow is sequential because emit cannot return before the collector's code returns. The producer can't start on the second value while the first one is still being posted, and inside one collection the collector never runs twice at once. That is also why the KDoc of FlowCollector says emit "is not thread-safe and should not be invoked concurrently". A plain call has nothing that would protect the collector from two callers at the same time.

A flow also gets backpressure for free. Backpressure means a slow consumer slows the producer down, so values don't pile up in memory. Reactive Streams needs a protocol for that. A flow needs nothing, because the producer is stuck inside emit until the consumer is done. Take a reader that needs 100 ms per settlement line and a ledger writer that needs 300 ms per posting. In virtual time, which is exact, both the toy and the real flow { } print:

t= 100 emit 1
t= 400 posted 1     <- emit(1) returns only now
t= 500 emit 2       <- 100 + 300 + 100
t= 800 posted 2
t= 900 emit 3
t=1200 posted 3     <- (100 + 300) x 3

The second emit happens at t=500, and it can't happen earlier: from 100 to 400 the producer was inside emit(1). In the restaurant, that's the cook standing at the table. Free backpressure has a price, and this is it: 1200 ms for three items, where the slower side alone needs only 900. Lesson 4 of this track adds a buffer to win some of that back, and pays for it in memory.

Stopping early goes through the same call. A collector that wants no more values, like the one behind take(2), has no handle on the producer's loop. All it can do is throw. The exception flies back up through emit, the producer's loop ends, and its finally blocks run on the way out. The real take does this with an internal exception, which the next lesson takes apart. You'll write the toy version in the lab.

Every number is a little later than the model, by a few milliseconds up to a few dozen on the first lines, because real sleeps overshoot and a cold JVM is slow at its first prints.

sections.h: The real Flow, and operators as collectors inside collectors
sections.html:
The library's two interfaces have the toy's shape. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 they are:

Java
// Java equivalent: java.util.concurrent.Flow, the JDK's Reactive Streams interfaces (abridged)
interface Publisher<T>  { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> subscriber); }
interface Subscription  { void request(long n); void cancel(); }
interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription subscription);
    void onNext(T item);
    void onError(Throwable throwable);
    void onComplete();
}
Kotlin
public interface Flow<out T> {
    public suspend fun collect(collector: FlowCollector<T>)
}

public fun interface FlowCollector<in T> {
    public suspend fun emit(value: T)
}

Only FlowCollector is a fun interface. That is how flow.collect { v -> ... } takes your lambda: Kotlin converts the lambda into a FlowCollector. Flow is a plain interface, so Flow { ... } does not compile ("interface ... does not have constructors"). That's on purpose. Its KDoc says Flow "is not stable for inheritance in 3rd party libraries", because new methods may be added to it later. Build flows with flow { }, or extend AbstractFlow, which is marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi.

Java's own java.util.concurrent.Flow works the other way round. The subscriber pulls: it calls request(n), and the publisher may send at most n more items. Kotlin's flow needs no such call, because the producer can't get ahead of a function call that hasn't returned yet.

Operators are flows built on flows. Here is map on the toy:

Java
// a default method in the Java ToyFlow interface
default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) {
    return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value)));
}
Kotlin
fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> =
    toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } }

Read it from the inside out. map returns a new flow. When that flow is collected, it collects the flow above it with a collector of its own, and that collector calls the next emit with the new value. It is a collector wrapped in a collector. filter is the same thing with an if around the emit. The library writes both in nearly the same way, as the next lesson shows. So a chain of five operators is five nested calls for each value. That's why the stack grew by one emit frame per map, and why operators need no locks or queues between them.

analogy: A plain flow is a restaurant with one cook and no counter. The recipe card (the flow) does nothing by itself. A meal is cooked only when a diner sits down and calls collect, and every new diner gets a fresh cooking session from the top. The cook plates a dish, walks it to the table and waits there while the diner eats, so the kitchen can never get ahead of the dining room. A waiter (an operator such as map) can stand between them, but he too walks each plate over and waits. The analogy breaks at the waiting. A real cook standing at a table is lost to the kitchen. A suspended coroutine holds no thread: while your collector is inside delay or a database call, the thread goes off and runs other coroutines, and only this one collection is stuck.
world: Picture a Kafka consumer wrapped in flow { }: it polls a batch, emits each payment event, and the collector writes ledger entries to Oracle. Each emit returns only after the ledger write, so the consumer never polls the next batch while the current one is half posted. If Oracle slows down, the whole flow slows with it, and you see that as growing consumer lag, not as memory filling up with events nobody has written. Two things follow. A long stall in the collector is also a long gap between polls, so keep the consumer's max.poll.interval.ms in mind. And a metric around emit in the consumer measures the ledger, not Kafka.
mistake:
The most common mistake is reading a timer around emit as the producer's own time. A settlement reader records read_ms around emit(record), the dashboard shows 300 ms per line, and someone spends a day tuning the CSV parser. The 300 ms belongs to the ledger writer: everything downstream runs inside that emit. People make this mistake because emit looks like queue.put. Time the work you own, and keep emit outside the timer:

Java
long start = System.nanoTime();
Record record = parse(line);                         // only the reader's work
metrics.record("read_ns", System.nanoTime() - start);
collector.emit(record);                              // the downstream's time, not ours
Kotlin
val start = System.nanoTime()
val record = parse(line)                             // only the reader's work
metrics.record("read_ns", System.nanoTime() - start)
emit(record)                                         // the downstream's time, not ours

compare.title: The toy flow in Java and Kotlin

java.title: ToyFlowJava.java (abridged)
java.html: // Java equivalent: a hand-written push flow. emit blocks the thread while the collector works. interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } ToyFlow<Integer> payments = collector -> { for (int id = 1; id <= 3; id++) collector.emit(id); }; payments.map(id -> id * 100).collect(v -> System.out.println("got " + v));

kotlin.title: ToyFlow.kt (abridged)
kotlin.html: fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } val payments = toyFlow { for (id in 1..3) emit(id) } payments.map { it * 100 }.collect { v -> println("got $v") }

compare.note: The shapes match line for line, and the calls happen in the same order. What differs is underneath. Java's emit blocks a thread while the collector works, so a thousand slow collections need a thousand threads. Kotlin's emit suspends a coroutine, and the thread is free during the wait. Java lets any interface with one abstract method take a lambda, so a lambda can be a ToyFlow. Kotlin asks for fun interface, and the real Flow leaves it out on purpose, which is why you build flows through flow { }. Kotlin also declares variance on the interfaces (out T on the flow, in T on the collector), where Java would write ? super T at every use.

worked.title: Write a toy operator that times the downstream

steps.say: The settlement dashboard says each line takes 300 ms to read. Before you tune the parser, write a toy operator that measures exactly what a timer around emit measures. It has the shape of map: collect the flow above, and wrap the call to the next emit.
steps.code: fun <T> ToyFlow<T>.timeDownstream(record: (value: T, took: Duration) -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = toyFlow { this@timeDownstream.collect { value -> val mark = TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow() // 1. start the clock emit(value) // 2. every operator below, and the collector record(value, mark.elapsedNow()) // 3. stop it when the downstream returns } }

alt.html: // a default method in the Java ToyFlow interface default ToyFlow<T> timeDownstream(BiConsumer<T, Long> record) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> { long start = System.nanoTime(); // 1. start the clock downstream.emit(value); // 2. everything below runs here record.accept(value, (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); // 3. stop it, in ms }); }

steps.say: Put it between a reader that needs 100 ms per line and a ledger writer that needs 300 ms per posting. In a real-time run it printed 300, 302 and 300 ms. That's the ledger's time. The reader's own 100 ms happens before emit and never shows up.
steps.code: toyFlow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit("pay-$i") } } // the reader .timeDownstream { id, took -> println("$id downstream took ${took.inWholeMilliseconds} ms") } .collect { delay(300) } // the ledger writer // pay-1 downstream took 300 ms // pay-2 downstream took 302 ms // pay-3 downstream took 300 ms

alt.html: ToyFlow<String> reader = collector -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { sleep(100); collector.emit("pay-" + i); } // the reader }; reader.timeDownstream((id, ms) -> System.out.println(id + " downstream took " + ms + " ms")) .collect(id -> sleep(300)); // the ledger writer

steps.say: Where you put it decides what it measures. Each operator in a plain flow sees, inside its emit, the time of everything below it. So moving the timer down the chain takes operators out of the number.
steps.code: reader.map { parse(it) }.timeDownstream(log).collect { ledger.post(it) } // the ledger only reader.timeDownstream(log).map { parse(it) }.collect { ledger.post(it) } // parse plus the ledger

alt.html: reader.map(r -> parse(r)).timeDownstream(log).collect(ledger::post); // the ledger only reader.timeDownstream(log).map(r -> parse(r)).collect(ledger::post); // parse plus the ledger

steps.say: The library's onEach has the same shape with your action in front of emit. In its source it is transform { value -> action(value); return@transform emit(value) }. On the toy it is one line:
steps.code: fun <T> ToyFlow<T>.onEach(action: suspend (T) -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = toyFlow { this@onEach.collect { value -> action(value); emit(value) } }

alt.html: default ToyFlow<T> onEach(Consumer<T> action) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> { action.accept(value); downstream.emit(value); }); }

lab.title: Build the toy flow and make take stop the producer
steps: Run the tests once. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. Read the test names in ToyFlowTest: they are the spec.
Write toyFlow and toList. Three tests turn green: running the body again, the event order, and the slow collector in virtual time.
Write map and filter as collectors wrapped in collectors. Don't collect into a list first. The event-order test checks that each value goes all the way down before the producer reads the next one.

Write take. Check count with require before you build the flow. Inside, make a fresh Any() as your marker, emit each value, and after the count-th one throw ToyAbortException(marker). Catch it around the upstream collect, and rethrow it if e.owner !== marker.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them once more.
hints: take can't return from the producer's loop, because that loop is someone else's code. Throwing from the collector is the only way out. The exception travels back through the producer's emit, which is why the producer's finally runs.
Compare markers with !==, which tests identity. Two Any() objects are never the same object, and that is the point of the marker.

If the nested-take test fails and your result has an extra 99 in it, your take catches every ToyAbortException. The inner take(3) swallowed the outer take(1)'s abort, so the outer body carried on and emitted 99.
Put require(count > 0) before return toyFlow { ... }, so a bad count fails when the flow is built, as it does for the library's take.

drill.title: Write the two interfaces from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In a blank file, write ToyCollector, ToyFlow, the toyFlow builder and map, with no imports from kotlinx.coroutines.flow. Then write two lines that prove the flow is cold. Check the variance: which interface gets out T, and which gets in T?

answer.html: fun interface ToyCollector<in T> { // it only takes values in suspend fun emit(value: T) } interface ToyFlow<out T> { // it only hands values out suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) } fun <T> toyFlow(block: suspend ToyCollector<T>.() -> Unit): ToyFlow<T> = object : ToyFlow<T> { override suspend fun collect(collector: ToyCollector<T>) = collector.block() } fun <T, R> ToyFlow<T>.map(transform: suspend (T) -> R): ToyFlow<R> = toyFlow { this@map.collect { value -> emit(transform(value)) } } // cold: building prints nothing, each collect prints "run" again val f = toyFlow { println("run"); emit(1) } runBlocking { f.collect { }; f.collect { } } // run, run

alt.html: // Java equivalent: the same shape with plain methods (no variance on the declarations) interface ToyCollector<T> { void emit(T value); } interface ToyFlow<T> { void collect(ToyCollector<T> collector); default <R> ToyFlow<R> map(Function<T, R> transform) { return downstream -> this.collect(value -> downstream.emit(transform.apply(value))); } } // cold: building prints nothing, each collect prints "run" again ToyFlow<Integer> f = c -> { System.out.println("run"); c.emit(1); }; f.collect(v -> { }); f.collect(v -> { }); // run, run

recap: A flow is two interfaces with one suspend function each: Flow.collect(collector) and FlowCollector.emit(value).
flow { } only stores your block. collect runs it, from the top, once per call. That is what cold means.
emit is a direct call into the collector. The collector's code runs inside emit, on the same stack and the same thread.
So a plain flow handles one value at a time, and a slow collector slows the producer: with 100 ms and 300 ms per item, the second emit is at t=500.
Operators like map and filter are collectors wrapped in collectors. A collector stops the producer by throwing back up through emit, so the producer's finally runs.
Only FlowCollector is a fun interface. Build flows with flow { }, because Flow is not stable for inheritance.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Our settlement reader is a flow, so it reads the file in the background and keeps lines in a buffer until the ledger writer catches up." Explain, from the call shape, what really happens.
explain.answer: There's no background work and no buffer in a plain flow. flow { } only stores the reader's code, and collect runs it in the collector's own coroutine. Each emit(line) is a direct call into the ledger writer's code, so the writer posts the line while the reader is still inside emit. Only when the posting returns does emit return, and only then does the reader read the next line. So the reader is never more than one line ahead, it runs on the same thread, and a slow ledger slows the reader down. If we want the reader to run ahead, we have to ask for it with an operator such as buffer or flowOn, and those add a second coroutine and a channel.

deeper.html:
A few details help when you read real stack traces and real code.

Line numbers in inlined frames can mislead. map is inline, so its collector's code is copied into your file, and the frame's file and line point into the library source it came from. They can even point past the end of that file. In one run, map's frame pointed at Emitters.kt:217. Trust the class name ($$inlined$map$1$2) more than the line.

flow.collect { } calls the member function Flow.collect, with your lambda converted into a FlowCollector. Older versions had an inline extension collect(action). It is still in 1.11.0, but marked @Deprecated(level = DeprecationLevel.HIDDEN) for JS and Native compatibility, so your code never calls it. In a stack trace your lambda appears as a generated class's emit method.

You can implement Flow yourself with object : Flow<T>. It compiles, and it behaves like the toy, with no checks at all. That's the reason not to. A hand-written Flow can call emit from another thread, or keep emitting after the collector failed, and nothing stops it. The next lesson shows the checks flow { } runs on every emit, and what goes wrong without them.

java.util.concurrent.Flow (JDK 9 and later) is the JDK's copy of the Reactive Streams interfaces. Its contract has rules a Kotlin flow gets from the call shape: a publisher must not send more items than were requested, and it must not call onNext from two threads at once. In a plain Kotlin flow the first rule is replaced by emit not returning, and the second holds because there is only one call at a time.
